extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics
extracted.subtask_short: truth of space in landscape painting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for painters on rendering truthful spatial relationships in landscape (foreground, middle distance, distance) through drawing, touch, and selective indistinctness rather than by colour alone. Emphasises how the eye focuses, how to treat foreground vs distance, and how to suggest detail without literal delineation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space indicated by drawing rather than hue
rubrics_metrics.description: Space is more clearly indicated by the drawing of objects than by their hue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing (degree to which details and parts are distinct or confused) is the most constant and certain criterion of distance; even when aerial tone is incorrect, correct drawing will produce genuine truth of space, while defective drawing will destroy all space however skilful the tint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of seeing unequal distances distinctly at once
rubrics_metrics.description: It is totally impossible to see distinctly, at the same moment, two objects, one of which is much farther off than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by the window-frame example: fix on near bars and distant objects become indistinct, and vice versa. This optical fact must inform painting: the artist cannot legitimately represent both near and far with equal distinctness because the eye does not receive them together so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either foreground or distance must be partially sacrificed
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting, either the foreground or distance must be partially sacrificed; if we represent near and distant objects as both giving distinct images, we violate nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the foreground is fully given, the distance must be reduced and vice versa: representing both with equal completeness is a gross falsehood (like showing four sides of a cube at once). The painter must decide where the eye's focus is and render accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decisive partial assertion of form, not slurred lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Indistinctness to express distance/retirement should not be achieved by slurred or soft lines (a vice), but by a decisive imperfection—a firm, but partial assertion of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's method: give enough suggestion of form so the eye feels proximity without allowing it to rest or cling to details. Examples: Copley Fielding's moorland foregrounds—broad wet sweeps that suggest without defining. Avoid slurring as mere laziness; indistinctness must be purposeful and precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-determination of foreground detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Overly determined, sharply finished foregrounds destroy the effect of space in a picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Callcott's Trent injured by harsh foreground figures; Stanfield and Harding often sacrifice space by making near forms too distinct. When the distance is the object of attention, foregrounds should be treated with controlled indistinctness to lead the eye to the middle and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for incompletely drawn figures when distance is focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Near figures may need to be rendered incompletely (e.g., 'round balls with four pink spots' for faces) when the picture's focus is on distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of drawing is necessary because if the eye is adapted to the distance it cannot perceive fully detailed near figures; completing such figures (e.g., having a figure-painter add eyes/feet) would destroy the truth of space and the beauty of the work. The incompleteness must be intentional, not from incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retirement (distance) causes confusion, not annihilation, of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: As objects recede, their individual details become confused and undecided but are not annihilated; they remain visible as texture or checkering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with the square/circle-on-paper test and the friend's face example: distant details blend into a rich but indistinct mass which still differs from a flat painted surface. Painters should render distant objects as confused yet texturally influential masses, not blank or featureless areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature is never distinct and never vacant; every touch should suggest more
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature always contains something that cannot be completely seen and something that can always be hinted; nothing in nature is either totally distinct or utterly vacant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore every touch which does not suggest more than it represents is false; every space that represents nothing is false. The painter must suggest more than he shows, creating mystery and abundance rather than either complete delineation or blankness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the old-masters' extremes (seeing everything or nothing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The landscapes of the old masters commonly err by either showing every leaf/brick distinctly (Dutch) or producing dead, vacant spaces (Italians); both contradict nature's rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Poussin's dead square masses and Claude's countable battlements or dead gray walls—both are false. Nature would present multitudinous intersections and spots that make a living, mysterious texture, not explicit countable elements or voids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painter's imperative of fulness and finish
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter must give as much fulness and finish as his means allow; he cannot excuse leaving parts vacant because he lacks a mile of space like nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occupy the inch: chisel the rock faithfully, tuft the forest delicately, then allow playful light. The painter must do the labor (careful study and detailed work) that underlies the delightful effects of light and atmosphere; play without prior work is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not vacancy; generalization should preserve unity of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth (generalization) is unity, not destruction of parts; it must not annihilate the truths of nature by removing details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True breadth results from arranging materials and concords of details into impressive masses; false breadth results from eclipsing details. The painter should generalise only by retaining the mysterious detail that composes the mass, not by blotting out particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turner's distances: every inch conceived, suggestive not explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner's distances are abundant yet each part suggests more than it represents; the conception of each inch is complete in the artist's mind but only partially given on canvas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Turner's work no atom lacks meaning though no line is fully made out; distances should be rich, various, and mysterious—each small area being a separate conceived picture but rendered so that it looks like natural distance to the careless eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural distance: suggest multitudinous texture rather than distinct lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Distant architecture should be rendered as a mass of multitudinous vertical lines and intersections—visible as symmetry and arrangement but not as countable, distinct elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Westminster Abbey from Highgate —you feel a multitude of vertical lines but cannot distinguish or count them. Avoid the architect's precise line-work (which makes a model, not a building) and Canaletto's dot-for-shadow approach (which yields vacancy). Aim for inextricable, visible richness that as a whole is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply mystery and inexhaustible finish even to near objects when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even near objects possess elements that cannot be fully seen and thus should be rendered with fulness and mysterious detail rather than crude explicitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature's ceaseless decoration (e.g., a weedy bank) exceeds human carving; painters should aim for delicate suggestion and richness in near detail rather than literal over-clarification. Exception: when botanical fidelity or close foreground attention is deliberately the subject, render details fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake playful light for substantive depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'play' of light and the adjuncts of atmosphere are not substitutes for the substantive labor of modelling and detailing the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After spending labour to model rock, river, and forest, the painter may indulge in frolics of light; but if he presents the play without the underlying work the picture is the 'play before the lesson'—an adjunct instead of the essence, and will not be pardoned.
